p: Okay.
We will be out addressing them.

And I guess especially this season, knowing that there is more of a need with resurfacing miles, streets master plan, and all of the pothole repairs, do you think that you'll be able to fully staff up, and how do you plan to address any needs in the future?

Yeah, well, the roadway division is the one division where we don't have any hiring problems. We in fact have about 36 applicants for every assistant city highway repair, uh, position that we have open. So we have full employment in the roadway division, so we do not expect any problems.

Are you looking to use technology training or deployment any differently to find efficiencies in its operations? I know that

these days it seems like the technology question is coming up a bit, but just wondering.

Yeah, so we are always looking to be on the cutting edge of asphalt work around the country. We are actually at the highest in the nation for using recycled asphalt, meaning we mill up the old street and we put it back into the mix. We're already at 40 percent, which is a great number, and we're looking to increase that in the coming months and years to perhaps as high as 50 percent. And we're also in the process of constantly upgrading our asphalt plant equipment in order to be able to be more innovative.

Perfect. And historically savings have been taken out at DOT in contracts, telecommunication maintenance, safety programs like Vision Zero. Is it expected that these areas will be featured in the CSO's proposals? And can you provide any examples of potential savings?

Yeah, we're still looking– our savings are due on Friday. I am the chief savings officer. We're looking at every program, but we're looking at areas where it is not going to be impacting any services delivered

to New Yorkers. So you're right, usually we find savings in future contracting, budget codes or efficiencies in PS savings, for example, which means, you know, we're just not hiring those folks. So, rest assured that I— we're going to do everything we can to make sure that we limit the impact to New Yorkers.

Yes, definitely don't want to cut services, especially now. And on the revenue side, anticipated revenue from franchises, bus stop, and other is expected to decrease by $12.3 million in fiscal '27, down to $52 million from $64.3 million in fiscal '26. So could you please briefly explain the scope of this revenue and why it is expected to decrease in the out years?

The targets that we set with OMB are usually pretty conservative targets. If you're talking about the JCDecaux [sic] revenue, that may be due to a deal we made with them where they essentially bring down the revenue but install more bus shelters across the city. That was done last fiscal year. We're in communication with OMB to see if they're going to do it again this fiscal year. But overall, we don't expect our revenue to significantly decrease on any

given program. In fact, most of the revenue is coming in a little higher.

Okay. Okay. And parking meter revenue– parking meters are the department's largest revenue source at $257.7 million, and New York City has more than 12,000 miles of curb encompassing over 3 million street parking spaces, but just 80,000 of these are metered, or fewer than 2.5 percent. So increasing metered street parking on commercial corridors— I just want to emphasize commercial corridors— could raise significant additional revenue for the city. The Center for an Urban Future has written that if the city were to meter just a quarter of existing free spaces, it could generate at least $1.21 billion in additional revenue. So do you support increased metering on commercial corridors, and have you done your own analysis on parking meter revenue?

I'll start by saying that, as I mentioned in my testimony, we are taking a hard look at our parking policy across the board. We know curb space is some of the most in-demand real estate in the city. But that said, pricing is just one of several tools that we can use. Things like

loading zones for deliveries or pickup and drop-off of passengers, micro distribution hubs for freight– so we're really looking across the board all the time. You know, that said, we know it's really frustrating for folks to have to circle looking for a spot, especially in commercial districts. It's actually not good for business either, right?
Right.

If customers have a hard time– and in addition, it's not great from a safety and pollution standpoint and all those other things. So, you know, I think we're always assessing our metering and where we have it. And, you know, as land uses change, should our metering change?

Okay. And do you see any anticipated issues or potential problems with doing it in, you know, additional commercial corridors? And what would that be? And I can say that for districts like mine, they're pretty much wanting to keep things like the residential parking because we don't have a lot of transit in the district and they do rely heavily on cars. It's very residential. So in terms of the commercial corridors though, if there's any anticipated issues you foresee?
Sorry to clarify, issues in terms of just being able to expand it?
Yeah.
No, I don't think there's issues in those kinds of expansions in commercial areas. Yeah.
Okay. And as always, we'd just like to emphasize that you engage obviously the community boards and the local folks in the area as well, especially the businesses.

I mean, I can just clarify, in the past when we've raised our parking meter rates, we haven't seen a huge pushback or issues, and we do notify the community boards, I believe at least 30 days before we do that. I would also– I think it's also worth mentioning that we have different zones for the city. It is not one size fits all. We charge depending on the area and the demand. So we don't expect any issues if we decide to go this route.

Okay. And I would emphasize instead of just notifying them 30 days before, if you could include them in the process for the feedback, that'd be great too. Because then I

feel like there's less pushback if you get their buy-in early. So, thank you. That's it, Chair.
Thank you. Going back to questions. The preliminary plan baselines $5 million starting in fiscal 2027 for new bus and bike lanes. What cost will the new $5 million per year in proposed funding cover?

I can start it and then Deputy Mayor– Deputy Mayor, I just gave you promotion– Deputy Commissioner Beaton can fill in. But we expect a lot of that to be— so there's about 20 headcount that we're going to be adding. Most of those would be planners and engineers to do a lot of the work behind the scenes. And then there's also TPS for increase in markings. A lot of that work that we do for bus lanes and bike lanes requires markings, and there may be some concrete work as well.
Is DOT hiring for this— for these new positions now so that the roles can be filled early in fiscal '27?

Yeah, yeah, we actually— we were just discussing that. Technically, they don't hit until fiscal '27,

but it does take a while to bring in folks. So we were— we have those postings opening– open now.

Alright, I'm now going to turn it over to questions on lane miles cost. We have the 12th snowiest winter on record here in New York City, so needless to say, our roads will be in need of a lot of maintenance and resurfacing work. However, according to the PMMR, the average cost to resurface a single lane mile costs DOT $221,693, a substantial 15 percent increase in just two years. In response to rising costs, DOT has stated that the cost of petroleum and the fluctuating cost of oil play a role in the cost of resurfacing lane miles. With global tensions causing a recent spike in oil, how will this play a role in DOT's resurfacing operations? And does DOT have a plan in place to keep costs down? And what is specifically planned to do?

Thank you, Chair. So the increase in costs that you cite were due to a number of factors. Yes, you mentioned petroleum prices, which have up to this present time fluctuated. We also have prevailing wage and salary increases in the mix, and then overall increase in some of the inputs that go into asphalt, gravel,

stone, and things of that nature. We are committed to doing 1,150 lane miles, and we do expect the price of petroleum, therefore, affecting our costs to fluctuate, probably increase, for reasons that we're all aware of in the coming months, but we are committed to figuring out those costs and committing to our lane mile target.
Is there a plan in place to keep costs down?
There are certain things beyond our control. We're constantly evaluating what's happening and we're watching it very carefully. Anything that we can possibly do, we would do.

On the topic of lane miles, DOT has continued to resurface less and less roads every single year— 1,200 in fiscal 2023, 1,176 in fiscal 2024 and only 1,167 in fiscal 2025. In the first four months of this fiscal year, DOT is already a few miles behind what was done last year. This is an essential service and function that DOT is supposed to be doing. What is causing the negative trend on lane surface— lane resurfacing?

Okay, I wouldn't call it a negative trend. As I mentioned, our lane mile target is 1,150, we will always meet our lane-mile target. It's not a perfectly precise science as to which streets are closed up or completed exactly at the end of the fiscal year. So sometimes we're over— we always try to be over— and sometimes it's by 20 miles, sometimes it's by 40 miles. Sometimes we also use that time to catch up on other jobs. We'll do large, like, wear and tear jobs. We'll catch up on speed humps, and we'll do other work that the agency needs to do once that we have met our lane-mile target.

In 2015, Mayor de Blasio announced an increase, $242 million, to repave 1,200 lane miles across the five boroughs through 2016, and 1,300 lane miles to be repaved by June 2017. Wouldn't you consider this a negative trend?
You know, we talk a lot about that. We actually think 1,150 is the right amount to balance and keeping our roads in a state of good repair.

It is a— I would consider that to be a negative number compared to the

2017 numbers, personally. Will this administration be less ambitious than the previous administration in completing lane miles?
I wouldn't— no, it would not. It won't.
So would that mean that you're committing to the 1,300 lane miles?
No, we're not committing to 1,300 lane miles, but we intend to keep our streets in a state of good repair.

And, Chair, there was— that, that was in the, the Blasio administration when those baseline funding were there. A lot of that were to catch up to the Bloomberg years where the agency was not getting the proper amount of funding. It's since leveled, and so the target of 1,150 miles is where we need to be. We essentially caught up where we needed to catch up.
So is the goal 1,150 moving forward?
Yes.
Which is a negative trend compared to 2017 numbers.
Because we caught up, correct.

And with the increasing need of, like, you know, the— with the weather conditions and on everything that's coming our way, I think we ought to be increasing those goals. I'm just curious, I know that the administration does not want to get to 1,300. I do. If we could get to 1,300, what would the cost look like for that?
Yeah, yeah, we can check and get back to you.
Thank you. Does DOT have sufficient funding to ensure that it is operating at full capacity? And how many staff work on resurfacing, and are more personnel needed?
Chair, you're asking about resurfacing specifically?
Yes.
Okay, we have over 1,000 people working on resurfacing. The division has something like 1,300 and about 1,100 are involved in resurfacing.
Are more personnel needed?
No.
How does DOT measure the condition of a road, and what factors are considered when determining whether corrective action needs to be taken? And how often do these assessments happen?

Yes, so we have a very robust street assessment unit which looks at every roadway in the City of New York about at once a year, a little bit— takes a little bit longer than a year to get through each roadway. We have a system where we look at cracking, potholes, push-ups, humps, every sort of asphalt condition that you can think of and a lot that you probably have never even thought of. And we evaluate the condition of that road. We have categories we put the roads into: good, fair, poor, and that informs which roadways we’ll schedule for resurfacing that year within each community board.
Would more personnel be needed to achieve 1,300 miles?
Yes.
Alright, I'm going to turn over my colleagues for questions. Council Member Schulman?

Thank you very much, and thank you, Commissioner. And I just want to give a shout out to Margaret Forgione, who I knew when she was a Manhattan rep for DOT. So, a couple of questions. One is, I know you've probably answered this. The $271 million you have for roadway maintenance, that's enough considering all the potholes that we have and everything else, and that will probably get more?
That's correct.

Okay. I also want to ask you, my understanding, just talking about universal daylighting, that DOT did a study in the previous administration on daylighting that showed that some intersections would not necessarily benefit from daylighting? That's what we were told.
At this point, we're focused on looking forward and really—
[interposing] Okay.
We want to work–
[interposing] So is it— so is it the case that some intersections might not be conducive to daylighting?
We think daylighting can take different forms in situations.
Okay.
And we try to incorporate it into all—

[interposing] I appreciate that. So let me talk about the school, the 15 miles per hour. Do we know sort of what the parameters are around each of the schools? Like, is it a couple of blocks? Is it like— how does that— how is that going to work?

Sure. So we start by focusing on the block that's immediately in front of the school, you know, the place where the most activity is happening with children. And then as we look at each school, we look to see if it makes sense to continue farther down the street, or whether there's any other treatments, which— like daylighting— that could be appropriate to do at the same time.

Okay, because offline there's a couple of schools in my district that— where there have been accidents, and the people— there's a lot of complaints about people speeding through around where the schools are. So offline, I'll talk to you, and I know I'm having a meeting with you guys soon anyways.
Absolutely.

So, and then enforcement. So let me talk about that because there are– you know, I think it's a good idea, number one. But the other is that there are people who speed who get tons of tickets and they feel it's the cost of doing business. So how do we deal with those individuals?

That's right. We— what we've seen is that there's a kind of troubling trend of folks who, you know, we found our automated enforcement programs are very, very effective. But there is that segment, right, that—
Right.

No matter how many violations they get, or maybe they

have a defaced plate, license plate, or things like that, you know, that challenges the program, right– challenges the goals of the program. So it's definitely something that's on our radar.

And Councilmember, one of the things that was in the governor's budget, it was a proposal for a city-led ISA program or Super Speeders program. We've been in conversations with both houses as well as the governor's office. We're in support of that legislation. So–
[interposing] Yeah, we've had— we've done a resolution, I believe, on that. So–
Again, and we'll definitely be looking to your support as we're hitting the stretch towards the finalization of the budget.
And if you can also let us know if there's legislation that would help in that regard from our end, please let us know.
Absolutely.
Okay, that's all the questions that I have for you. That was easy, right? So thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Council Member Louis?

Thank you, Chair. I have a couple of questions, so if I could be added for the second round, but my first one is on outdoor dining. Now that outdoor dining is moving toward a year-round program, there are many concerns with DOT's ability to successfully execute this program. So I wanted to know, does the Preliminary Plan address the needs and concerns for our businesses— our business community regarding backlog and complicated application process? And does DOT require additional funds to hire more staff to process applications?

Thank you, Council Member. So DOT is very committed to the success of outdoor dining. This has become a beloved program within the city, and we're looking forward to— should it become year-round— making sure that is successful. Right now we have over 3,000 applications and restaurants in the program. We do have enough staff to continue should we get an influx of further

applications, to process everybody that's already working with us as well as any increased applicants.
Okay. And how much PS funding is currently budgeted in fiscals 2026 and 2027 and beyond for inspection and enforcement for staffing costs?
It's about $1.3 million. I think, if I remember correctly. We have about 10 plan reviewers and–
[interposing] That's for '26 and '27.
We have for '26. We're in conversations to make sure that we have the proper funding in '27 and beyond.
And I can talk a little bit about the enforcement. We have 10 people dedicated to enforcement of dining out. In fiscal '25, there were about 3,400 violations issued for this program.

Okay, and I think I have one more question I could quickly ask. DOT's capital commitment plan totals $14.3 billion across FYs '26 to FY '30. Is any portion of this funding allocated towards structural analysis, plaza

reconstruction, or pedestrian improvements, particularly at Newkirk Plaza? And if not, what is preventing the project from being included?

Council Member, let me check on Newkirk to see if it's in the five-year window, but a lot of that funding is in fact street reconstruction, so it usually has ped expansions, plaza— the plaza actually has a lump sum that we use for capital funding. Let me just check back on Newkirk. I just don't know if it's in the pipeline or not, but I can give you a timeline if it is.

And one more quick question on Newkirk. Given that Newkirk Plaza involves overlapping jurisdiction between DOT and the MTA, does DOT have any dedicated budget or capital coordination mechanism to advance projects that are stalled due to interagency responsibility disputes?
Yeah, so it's obviously a very complicated location with the MTA structure.
I’m aware.

But what we are committed to maintaining it and making sure that's

taken care of. We do that through our maintenance contract that takes care of plazas all over the city. So we have been incorporating that into it, which is separate from the capital question that we'll get back to you on. But we are committed to taking care of the space and making sure it stays clean.
I look forward for feedback because they've been waiting for years for this support and haven't received it. So I hope we could get it done this year.
I understand.
Thank you, Chair.
You don't have any other questions? You have more time.
Not right now, thank you.
Okay. Council Member Wong?

Thank you, Chair. I have a picture here, if you can see it, but this is not– this is not a crater on Mars or on the moon. This is a crater in my district, Queens Boulevard and Grand Avenue. It's been there since the last ice storm. And I lost track of the 311 calls because I

made at least two myself. It's still not fixed. Here's my question– potholes are one of the most common complaints my office receives. Some neighborhoods see quick responses while others deal with the same roadway hazards for months. The crater I show you, about 100 feet away, all— everything else was fixed except this one. So here's my question: why does it take so long for certain potholes to be repaired in some parts of the city? And what is DOT doing to improve repair times? Please talk.

Thank you. Very important question. We do need to make sure our roads are in safe and smooth condition. Typically it takes us about two days to repair a pothole. Obviously, now in a time like this, it might take a little bit longer. It sounds to me— and I'd like to connect with you on your condition— sounds to me like that condition could be something larger, a sinkhole or something of that nature. So sometimes we find that underground there's something washing away the roadway. And that sort of issue takes longer to address because we can't just throw asphalt on top of that condition, it will continue to sink. So instead, we work with maybe utilities, maybe with DEP, in

order to assess exactly what's happening there to get a proper fix. So if you get me that location, I will be sure to get back to you.
Yeah, it's— again, it's been there since the last ice storm, Grand Avenue and Queens Boulevard, my district.
Okay.

My second question is about milling and paving, repaving. My constituents frequently report roads being milled But then it takes two months for the repaving to happen, or some other extended periods of time, leaving rough and dangerous driving conditions. What— why is the lag time between milling and final repaving increased in recent years? It wasn't like this 10 years ago, five, 10 years ago. And do you have the average time between milling and paving? Thank you.

Okay, thank you. So there's a very important reason why we have a lag between milling and paving. That's an opportunity for all of the utilities, other city agencies, even homeowners with any kind of plumbing issues to come out. And while the street is what we call open, make those repairs, get in subsurface in

order to fix any issues, and then we can come back and have a perfect street and we can pave it all at one time. The alternative is having people make cuts at different times and cut into a freshly paved street, which is not something that we want. The vast majority of our roadways are paved two weeks after being milled. Sometimes you'll find a longer time period if those repairs do need to take longer, or sometimes we have more streets that we're attending to and we have weather, and we don't get back as quickly as we would like to.

Okay, thank you. And I have some more time. Last question– streetlights. Many blocks in my district have only one or two streetlights, so when one goes out, the entire block can become dangerously dark. I have cases where DOT looked at it and said, oh, it's a Con Edison problem. Con Edison comes, look at it, oh, it's a DOT problem. I get the runaround. My office gets the runaround. That was before I got elected. Alright? So, what is your solution to that? Because, we have several of these in my district.

Okay, so when it's a pretty simple matter of changing the

bulb in a streetlight, that gets done pretty quickly. The more tricky situation is when we have a problem. Sometimes we have no current, meaning there is no electricity coming to that light, or there could be something more problematic at the base of the streetlight, which might mean we need to swap out the streetlight and bring in a new one. We do not want you to ever be getting the runaround, you or any member of the public or anybody. So if you do see that condition, what we do is we will call Con Ed. We will stay on top of those discussions with them and make sure if it is a problem with the current, with the electrical current coming in, that we do have it done in a timely fashion, and then we can get it back on for you. Commissioner?

Yeah, I just want to add kind of bigger picture. I definitely— I'll say in almost every meeting I think I've had since being appointed, I've heard about frustrations with street lighting. So, I definitely hear that and I hear that frustration. We know that it's really such a bread and butter issue for a lot of communities, and it's something that I'll be personally taking a close look at.
Okay, I'll kind— I'll reach out for these runarounds that I've been dealing with six, seven months.
Councilman—
[interposing] Thank you.
You're wrapped up? Council Member Hanif?

Hi, everyone. So I'd like to first start by thanking you for finally closing the concrete recycling facility in the Columbia Waterfront District in my neighborhood. And of course, going back to what you shared about paving and milling and using our city's concrete and putting it back into our streets and wherever else is a valid– and like, that's what we should be doing. It's an environmental justice issue. However, at the same time, I know that the space to do that work is limited for DOT. Now with concrete recycling facility shut down for that specific work, what are you all thinking in terms of the future of ensuring that this really dusty and health risk project— projects are not happening in residential communities?

Yeah, thanks, Council Member. We always want to be good neighbors. We do have a lot facilities across the city. You're talking about the concrete recycling operation. We were— I'll just give a little history. We moved there on a temporary basis due to the South Brooklyn Marine Terminal wind turbine project. We did find a permanent home in an industrial area. So we expect to resume recycling— the concrete recycling operation very soon. And just to clarify, the concrete recycling is all of the work that we do in our sidewalk work. The recycling of the asphalt is something a little different.
Got it.
We also recycle that, but the facility you were referring to is the concrete recycling, and we're very excited to be able to turn on that machine.
And so for the future of this work, where— is there a dedicated site that DOT has, or is–
Yes, it's in Metropolitan Avenue in a pretty industrial area in between Queens and Brooklyn.

Okay, great, great to hear that. I want to talk about delivery workers and the– specifically the e-bike trade-in program. How many delivery workers does DOT expect the $1.4 million e-bike trade-in allocation to serve, and what is the estimated cost per participant?

I'll talk about the cost, and then I can turn it over to the Commissioner about the policy. The cost that you see in the Preliminary Budget was something that we were– that we already spent last fiscal year.
Okay.

And so this is just a repayment from that amount. But we were very excited about the program. I think it helped over 400 delivery workers to provide— to get brand new e-bikes. But it also provided a lot of training for delivery workers, not just the ones that got the e-bikes but more delivery workers. So I can turn it over to the Commissioner if he wants to add anything else.

Sure. I'll just say, you know, on the general topic of e-bikes safety and delivery worker safety, I think as the mayor said,

we're taking kind of a worker-forward approach. It's a tough job. We're working closely with our sister agencies like DCWP to promote safe operation. We had created our Sustainable Delivery Unit last year, and they've really been deeply engaged in this issue. We're looking at potential legislation. But I think we're– you know, we're— and we're doing quite a bit of education as well to the workers and to—

[interposing] Absolutely, which is greatly appreciated. And I've been able to partner with the DOT to do some work in my district, and really grateful. Now, Coming to bike storage and parking– in my district, the Kensington community is where large swaths of delivery workers live, and they serve the Fifth Avenue and Seventh Avenue corridors, restaurant corridors, local commercial corridor, and in all of those areas there is insufficient placement for their bikes. Now, that creates a risk for these workers to get fines, or to just be situated in an unsafe space. So, I'd like to know what the plan is to address— to make sure that they have safe parking space, and that even if they— I mean, I don't think anyone should be putting their e-bikes in their homes. The city must have a plan for

this. I'd like to know what is the cost or what funding are you all allocating towards this specific important urgent need?

Thank you, Council Member. Yeah, we completely agree. You know, when you hear about the challenges that cyclists face, having a secure safe place to park is that towards the top of the list, right? And that's why we're really excited we finally got the funding in the January budget to launch a secure bike parking program. That's going to allow us to install and maintain 500 locations over the next five years. And that's actually on top of the over 2,000 standard bike racks we do every year. So I think you're going to see a real c-change in how we're providing safe bike parking. But, you know, we're– we'd love to work with the council to identify other ways that we can increase bike parking.

Thank you, council member. Want to now turn over the topic of potholes. Maintaining the quality of the city's roads, thoroughfares, and highways during the winter season are integral to motorists, cyclists, and public transportation riders. Despite this, in the first

four months of fiscal— of this fiscal year, DOT crews repaired 5.1 percent fewer potholes on local streets, and the arterial highway system when compared to the same period in fiscal 2025. Additionally, the PMMR also shows in fiscal 2024 DOT repaired a total of 154,898 potholes on local streets and arterials, which reflected a 12.4 percent decrease from fiscal '23. This reflects another downward trend that DOT is falling behind on. More recently, this failure has turned deadly. A 46-year-old man was thrown to his death after hitting a pothole while reading— while riding a motorized scooter in Ozone Park, Queens last week. It was only after he was pronounced dead at Jamaica Hospital DOT crews came by and filled the pothole. I assume after the winter we had— I assume after the winter we had the roads are in desperate needs of maintenance. What is the reason for the decline in repairing potholes?

I'll start and feel free First Deputy Commissioner. So I think as First Deputy Commissioner Forgione said, filling potholes is— there's a lot of– it’s dynamic, right? It depends on the specific weather conditions of that winter. We can't fill potholes when there's snow on the ground

or the ground is frozen. But even bigger picture, potholes are kind of a symptom, and what we really wanna do is try to address the underlying problem. But when there are potholes, we respond to them very quickly, typically under two days. And you know, when we see kind of a proliferation of potholes after a winter weather, then we do a blitz like we did on Saturday.

We'll get into the blitz shortly. I have a set of questions on that. Is your staffing equal to— with— within the pothole, the division, is your staff equal to your ratio of work? Joe Puglio, President of Local 983 of District Council 37, recently said in regards to fixing potholes, “We just don't have the manpower to do the job in a timely manner.” Do you agree with Mr. Puglio? If not, why not?
